⚡️ Pezeshkian says 5% cut in electricity consumption saved Iran up to $10 billion

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran has reduced electricity consumption by 5% compared with last year, saving between $5 billion and $10 billion, President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Sunday.

Speaking at a meeting with preachers and clerics, Pezeshkian said improved energy consumption patterns had helped strengthen the country’s economic resilience and reduced its dependence on imported fuel.
​
“With this level of savings compared with what we consumed last year, we have now managed to save between $5 billion and $10 billion,” he said.
​
Pezeshkian said lower energy consumption had also reduced the country’s need to import fuel and gasoline, helping the government manage domestic demand and ensure adequate supplies.
​
He urged households and businesses to contribute to further reductions in electricity, water, gasoline and natural gas consumption, arguing that energy conservation was essential to supporting domestic production.
​
“We have no right to cut electricity supplies needed by industrialists and businesses,” he said, adding that maintaining production and employment remained a government priority.
​
The president warned that disruptions to industrial activity and rising unemployment could provide opportunities for Iran’s adversaries to exploit public dissatisfaction.
​
Pezeshkian said the government has adopted economic measures to maintain supplies of essential goods and medicines despite restrictions on trade and financial transactions caused by US sanctions.
​
He also stressed the importance of expanding economic and trade relations with neighboring countries and other international partners to improve living conditions.
​
Pezeshkian said the government was seeking to address economic challenges through more effective management and cooperation across public institutions.

The Real Question of 2028 🏛: Can America Move Beyond Trump?


The 2028 presidential election is still two years away, but the political battle to define America's future has already begun.

The Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms have given the party a renewed opportunity to challenge Republican dominance. Yet taking control of Congress does not answer the more difficult question: what exactly do Democrats want America to become?

The party faces a strategic dilemma. Moving toward the political center could attract independent voters and disillusioned Republicans. Embracing a more progressive agenda could energize younger voters and the party's activist base. But neither strategy guarantees a winning presidential coalition.

Republicans face a different problem. Trump remains the defining figure of the modern Republican Party, but his political model raises an important question about succession. 

Can MAGA survive as a coherent movement without Trump himself? And can a future Republican candidate preserve its appeal without reproducing the political divisions that have made it so controversial?

The deeper issue is that both parties risk becoming trapped by the political identities of the past decade. Democrats define themselves largely in opposition to Trump, while Republicans continue to measure political loyalty against his personal influence. 

The real opportunity in 2028 may belong to the candidate who breaks this cycle. America does not necessarily need another political personality capable of dominating the national conversation. It needs a credible answer to a more difficult question: what should American power, prosperity and democracy look like after the Trump era?

That may be the most consequential contest of 2028...
